messages:
maya: Quick datapoint from the 02:00 perf run — kernel reorder patch reduced p95 for short sequences (<=64) by ~15%, nice. However, KV cache hit-rate on the same traffic mix dropped ~8% which pushed median latency up for requests that rely on cached prefixes.

thomas: Ugh, that tradeoff was my worry. Do we have a profiling trace showing whether larger continuous batches are aggregating mixed prefixes and evicting warm entries?

maya: Yep, attached a short snippet from flameprof (trimmed):

```
seq<=64: p95 114ms -> 97ms after kernel reorder
kv_cache: hit_rate 0.72 -> 0.66 (same window)
queueing: avg wait 9ms -> 13ms (continuous batching enabled)
batch_size_distribution: mean 18 -> 26 (more mixing across clients)
```

alex: That batch_size jump is telling. Continuous batching picks up more inflight requests and mixes prefixes. When mixed prefixes share a batch we lose KV reuse because the warmup pattern (same prefix repeated) is diluted.

samir: Can we quantify how much of the hit-rate drop is due to eviction vs mismatched keying? Two failure modes: 1) cache entries evicted earlier because bigger batches increase KV memory churn, 2) cache lookups miss because keys are salted by something in the request path.

maya: I instrumented per-key lifetime and saw eviction spikes aligning with large tail batches. Keying looks stable (we don't accidentally include timestamp). So eviction + slower warmup for newly-seen prefixes is the main culprit.

daphne: Hypothesis: continuous batching increases effective working set by merging prefixes from many users, so our LRU window can't keep hot prefixes warm. Two mitigations: affinity slicing (grouping by prefix hash) or warmstart seeding (proactively warming KV for expected hot prefixes).

thomas: Affinity slicing seems lower-risk. We could implement a lightweight prefix-hash routing inside the batcher: when forming a batch, prefer slots whose prefix_hash % N == shard_id. That will reduce cross-prefix mixing at the cost of slightly lower batch fill for low QPS shards.

alex: Agreed. Another idea is adaptive max_batch_delay: when we detect many unique prefixes in the pending queue, reduce the delay so batches are smaller and more prefix-homogeneous. If the prefix-uniqueness metric is low, increase delay to favor throughput.

maya: I sketched a quick experiment harness to simulate production mix and measure p50/p95 + cache hit-rate under 4 configs: baseline, kernel-reorder-only, kernel-reorder+affinity-slice, kernel-reorder+adaptive-delay. Command to run locally: 

```bash
# simulate 10k requests/s mix, 60s window
./bench_tool --clients 1000 --qps 10000 --mix profile.yaml --duration 60 \
  --runtime-config runtime.json --measure kv_hit_rate --out run1.json
```

samir: Nice. What does profile.yaml look like? Need to ensure realistic prefix skew (some prefixes very hot, long tail of uniques).

maya: profile.yaml: hot_prefixes: 12 (zipf theta 1.05), long_tail: base 0.01 unique/new per req. I can push the harness and configs to the perf branch.

thomas: Before we run everything, can we add one lightweight metric at runtime: prefix-cardinality per second (distinct prefix count / sec) and avg per-prefix request rate. That will let us trigger adaptive-delay rules in production later.

alex: Also keep an eye on kernel selection interactions. The kernel reorder that reduced p95 did so by swapping a faster matmul kernel that favors short sequences, but it slightly increased memory pressure per worker which can amplify KV evictions under high mixing. We should measure resident set size (RSS) and per-GPU memory alloc peaks during the bench.

maya: Good call — I added sampling: rss_peak_mb and kv_cache_entries metrics to the bench. Preliminary run: affinity-slice config recovered ~6% of hit-rate (0.66 -> 0.70) and p95 improved relative to kernel-only case. adaptive-delay recovered ~5% but with slightly higher median latency due to smaller batches.

daphne: So affinity-slice wins for hit-rate and tail latency? That matches my expectation: better locality preserves warm KV entries. But it's not free — implementation complexity and potential uneven throughput across shards.

samir: For canary, let's keep kernel reorder + affinity-slice as the rollout candidate. We should add telemetry: per-shard fill-rate, prefix-cardinality, kv_hit_rate, p50/p95. If shard fill-rate drops below 50% for >5min for a customer, fallback to global batching for them.

thomas: Agreed. Also add an AB test flag so we can compare production with matched traffic. Diff will be small but measurable.

maya: I'll open a PR with the batcher change (prefers grouping by prefix_hash modulo N where N is dynamic based on concurrency). Also include a flag to toggle adaptive-delay. PR will include bench results and the perf harness.

alex: Can you add a short note in the PR describing risks: potential skew and how fallback works? I'll review the kernel memory notes and make sure kernel tuner can be rolled back if memory impacts degrade.

maya: Yup. PR link when ready.

ci-bot: Build queued for branch: perf/affinity-slice — job #421 triggered.

samir: After rollout let's plan a 24h observation window and then measure customer-facing SLOs. If we see any >2% uplift in request error/latency for any tenant, we'll roll back.

daphne: Also, add a short explainer for SRE on how to interpret the new prefix-cardinality metric. They asked for a quick runbook for rollback.

maya: Will do. TL;DR: kernel reorder helped short-seq p95, but continuous batching mixed prefixes causing KV churn. Affinity-slicing wins in bench by preserving KV locality while keeping most of the kernel improvements. Next: PR + canary + 24h observation. :rocket:
